title: Fixed-anchor endomorphisms extend along iterated functorial span completions
statement:
Let $\mathcal C$ be a category [def-nagata-category], let $W$ be a wide subcategory (it contains every object and identity and is closed under composition) satisfying two-out-of-three: if two of $f,g,gf$ lie in $W$, so does the third. Let $U\subseteq W$ be a wide subcategory. Fix a functorial square-completion rule $S$: for each span $D\xleftarrow{q}B\xrightarrow{h}B'$ with $q\in U$, it chooses $D\xrightarrow{k}D'\xleftarrow{q'}B'$ with $q'\in U$ and $kq=q'h$. On every commuting triple of maps of input spans it chooses a map of output vertices commuting with $k,q'$, and these choices preserve identities and composition. Fix $n\geq0$, a chain $B_0\xrightarrow{h_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{h_n}B_n$, and $q_0:B_0\to D_0$ in $U$. Recursively let $(D_j,k_j:D_{j-1}\to D_j,q_j:B_j\to D_j)$ be the output of $S$ on $(D_{j-1}\xleftarrow{q_{j-1}}B_{j-1}\xrightarrow{h_j}B_j)$ for $1\leq j\leq n$. For every endomorphism $e_0:D_0\to D_0$ with $e_0q_0=q_0$, there is a specified sequence $e_j:D_j\to D_j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, whose $j$th term is the output-vertex map of $S$ on the input-span endomorphism $(e_{j-1},1_{B_{j-1}},1_{B_j})$. Every one of these input-span endomorphisms is well-defined, and
$$e_jq_j=q_j,\qquad e_jk_j=k_je_{j-1}\quad(1\leq j\leq n).$$
Moreover $e_j\in W$ for every $0\leq j\leq n$.

source.place: Dwyer–Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, Proposition 8.2(i), printed p. 29 (PDF p. 13), following Proofs paragraph; explicit auxiliary assertion extracted from the square-criterion proof step 5. No Stacks tag is claimed.

proof.text: For each $j$, the recursively chosen leg $q_j$ belongs to $U$: this holds for $j=0$ by hypothesis and passes from $q_{j-1}$ to $q_j$ by the output condition on $S$. Thus every object-level span completion in the statement is defined, and $q_j\in W$ since $U\subseteq W$. At stage zero the given $e_0$ satisfies $e_0q_0=q_0$. Applying the assumed two-out-of-three property to $q_0$, $e_0$ and $e_0q_0=q_0$ shows $e_0\in W$.

source.place: Proposition 8.2(i) and following Proofs paragraph, printed p.29 (PDF p.13); explicit elementary expansion of the fixed-anchor induction.

proof.text: Inductively suppose $e_{j-1}:D_{j-1}\to D_{j-1}$ has been specified and $e_{j-1}q_{j-1}=q_{j-1}$, where $1\leq j\leq n$. The triple $(e_{j-1},1_{B_{j-1}},1_{B_j})$ is a map from the $j$th input span to itself: its first square commutes because $e_{j-1}q_{j-1}=q_{j-1}1_{B_{j-1}}$, and its second because $1_{B_j}h_j=h_j1_{B_{j-1}}$. Define $e_j:D_j\to D_j$ to be the output-vertex map assigned to this triple by the given rule $S$. The two output squares supplied by that rule are exactly $e_jk_j=k_je_{j-1}$ and $e_jq_j=q_j1_{B_j}=q_j$. This proves the inductive invariant and specifies the next term without any further choice.

source.place: Proposition 8.2(i) and following Proofs paragraph, printed p.29 (PDF p.13); explicit elementary expansion of the fixed-anchor induction.

proof.text: For each newly constructed stage $j$, use $q_j\in W$ from Step 1 and $e_jq_j=q_j$ from Step 2. The arrow $q_j$ and the composite $e_jq_j$ both lie in $W$, so the assumed two-out-of-three property gives $e_j\in W$. Finite induction through $j=n$ therefore supplies all specified terms, all input-span endomorphisms and both asserted equations. When $n=0$ no successor step is required; the given $e_0$ and Step 1 already give the entire conclusion.
